study_identification_part.si4_title: GPT-based normative models of brain sMRI correlate with dimensional psychopathology

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: This study investigates whether a normative architecture composed of VQ-VAE and GPT models can detect psychiatric symptoms and disorders from brain structural MRI of youths, by examining associations between brain regions and CBCL symptom groups, ADHD scores, and ASD diagnosis.

rci1_dataset_name.reason: The paper clearly states that ABCD dataset was used for training normative models. The training was performed exclusively on typically developing subjects from ABCD dataset with CBCL scores in the lower three quartiles.
rci1_dataset_name.supporting_text: "The subjects of ABCD were split into three sets for training (n=6,756), validation (n=751), and testing (n=3,524) purposes. The CBCL total score was used as split criteria in the following manner. First, the examples were labeled as normal CBCL score (three lower CBCL quartiles) or high CBCL score (upper fourth CBCL quartile). Then, we assigned 10% of the normal and 100% of the high CBCL subjects to the test set. From the remaining 90% of normal CBCL subjects, one-tenth of the examples were assigned to validation and nine-tenths to the training set." (Supplement L8-L12); "models are normative, trained exclusively with TD subjects" (Supplement L9)

nm3_modeling_method.answer: Deep generative normative modeling using Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) and Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT); Ensemble of 9 GPT models from different serialization views
nm3_modeling_method.reason: The modeling method is extensively described in both the main text and supplementary materials. The architecture consists of two models: VQ-VAE for dimensionality reduction and tokenization, and GPT for modeling probability density function of typical brains.
nm3_modeling_method.supporting_text: "The architecture is composed of two models, a VQ-VAE... and a GPT (also known as an autoregressive Transformer)... The VQ-VAE learns a latent discrete representation of the brain, while the GPT models the likelihood of occurrence of each discrete element" (Main text L85-88); "During the VQ-VAE learning process, the input data go from nearly 14.2 million voxels to 16.1 thousand latent discrete codes. The reduced dimension of this latent discrete representation allows the training of GPT that models the likelihood of occurrence of each discrete element" (Supplement L17-19); "we reordered the latent representations generated by the VQ-VAE to train multiple GPT models (based on different views of the input data). After training, we had nine GPT models each obtained from a specific view of the serialized latent representations. Then, the predictions from these models were averaged in an ensemble to evaluate the test samples" (Supplement L18-21)

nm5_response_variable.answer: Likelihood of typicality (voxel-level, ROI-level, and whole-brain); derived from VQ-VAE tokenized brain segments processed by GPT
nm5_response_variable.reason: The response variable is the likelihood of typicality predicted by the GPT models for brain segments. These likelihoods are computed at voxel level, aggregated to ROI level using AAL3 atlas, and summed (log-likelihoods) for whole-brain typicality score.
nm5_response_variable.supporting_text: "The trained network predicts the likelihood of typicality of the downsized and quantized brain segments, where each VQ-VAE quantized brain segment... corresponds to a specific serialized GPT vocabulary token" (Main text L91-94); "The typicality score of the whole brain is calculated from the sum of all tokens' likelihood logarithms" (Supplement L23); "the likelihoods (per voxel) are averaged by each ROI of the brain atlas, producing per-ROI brain maps of likelihood" (Supplement L28-30)

The evaluation uses simple correlations and AUC analyses with Bonferroni correction but does not account for potential confounders.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Answer: Whole-brain typicality likelihood correlated with social problems (ABCD) and discriminated ASD diagnosis (ABIDE-II, AUC=0.60); multiple brain ROIs showed significant associations with CBCL symptom groups, ADHD scores, and ASD diagnosis after correction for multiple comparisons.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Answer: In the ABCD test set (n=3,524), whole-brain typicality likelihood significantly correlated with CBCL social problems (corrected p=0.006). ROI-level analysis revealed significant correlations for total, externalizing, rule-breaking, aggressive, conduct, and social problem subscales, primarily in cortical regions including superior parietal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, precuneus, cuneus, and occipital regions (Table 3). In BHRCS (n=737), ROI-level correlations were found for social, thought, somatic, depression, anxiety, internalizing, and total scores, exclusively in subcortical structures including cerebellar lobules, thalamus ventral posterolateral, ventral tegmental area, and red nucleus (Table 4). For ADHD-200 (n=922), significant correlations with inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity scores were found in cortical (superior frontal gyrus, anterior cingulate cortex) and subcortical regions (cerebellum, amygdala, substantia nigra); substantia nigra pars compacta was the only region correlating with ADHD index (Table 5). For ASD in ABIDE-II (n=580), whole-brain likelihood discriminated ASD diagnosis (AUC=0.60, p<0.001), with ROI-level AUC values ranging from 0.569 to 0.627, including insula, cingulate gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, postcentral gyrus, putamen, temporal regions, cerebellum, thalamus, and anterior cingulate cortex (Table 6). Whole-brain likelihood also correlated with age in BHRCS (r=-0.07), ADHD-200 (r=-0.19), and ABIDE-II (r=-0.33), but not in ABCD test set (r=-0.01), suggesting potential age confounding in out-of-distribution datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Answer: This is the first study to successfully assess all dimensional groups of CBCL symptoms from all brain regions based exclusively on structural MRI using GPT-based normative models. The approach demonstrates several advantages: 1) Same trained model can estimate different psychiatric conditions from distinct datasets as atypicals are detected as deviations from learned typicality; 2) Whole-brain assessment without bias to prior hypotheses; 3) Captures heterogeneity of individual differences without requiring consistent neurobiological signatures; 4) Transformer-based models robust to mapping input data relationships regardless of distance. Authors suggest future improvements: conditioning models by demographic information and confounders (comorbidities, scanner models); applying likelihood ratio to emphasize in-distribution semantic components; extending to other imaging modalities (functional MRI) for better estimates.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Answer: 1) Modest statistical effect sizes limit clinical diagnostic utility, though the approach is suitable for mapping brain-symptom associations. 2) Different demographic distributions (especially age range) between training (ABCD) and test datasets (BHRCS, ADHD-200, ABIDE-II) affected result replicability and correlation directions. 3) No control for scanner/site effects despite multi-site data with varied acquisition parameters (3T vs 1.5T, different manufacturers), potentially reducing effect sizes and generalizability. 4) Subject comorbidities were not analyzed as potential confounders due to lack of available information. 5) Age confounding evident in whole-brain associations in out-of-distribution datasets (BHRCS, ADHD-200, ABIDE-II). 6) Non-replication of findings across datasets (cortical regions in ABCD vs subcortical in BHRCS) likely due to age distribution differences and scanner parameter variations.

- general_notes.Answer: "Dataset-specific details: ABCD data collected from 21 sites in USA using multi-brand 3T scanners (acquisition parameters at https://abcdstudy.org/images/Protocol_Imaging_Sequences.pdf). ADHD-200 from 8 sites with head coils 8-32 channels, mostly 3T (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/adhd200/). ABIDE-II from 19 sites, mostly 3T scanners (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/abide_II.html). BHRCS from 2 Brazilian cities using exclusively 1.5T Signa HD and HDX (G.E. manufacturer); acquisition parameters in Sato et al. 2016. Only baseline/first collection data used. Subjects <20 years selected. Model architecture: VQ-VAE reduces 14.2 million voxels to 16.1 thousand latent discrete codes, serialized for GPT training. Nine GPT models trained on different serialization views and averaged in ensemble. 50 training epochs used. Code publicly available at https://github.com/SergioLeonardoMendes/normative_psychiatry. Experiments on NVIDIA DGX-2 server (16 GPU TESLA V100-SXM332GB) in Docker. BHRCS screening protocol prioritized participants with higher psychiatric disorder risk, explaining higher CBCL scores vs ABCD (27.1±25.2 vs 18.1±17.9). Age range differences critical: ABCD 9.9±0.6 years (narrow), BHRCS 9.9±1.9 years, ADHD-200 11.7±3.0 years, ABIDE-II 12.1±3.2 years (wider ranges). Scanner field strength difference: ABCD/ADHD-200/ABIDE-II mostly 3T providing better SNR and contrast vs BHRCS exclusively 1.5T. Authors note that likelihood ratio technique and demographic conditioning could improve future models."
